hook: The first bug was… a real insect?
fact: In 1947, Grace Hopper’s team found a moth stuck inside the Harvard Mark II computer.
detail: They taped it into the logbook: “First actual case of bug being found.”
source: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

fact: Ada Lovelace wrote the first computer program in 1843, for a machine that was never built.
detail: It calculated Bernoulli numbers on Charles Babbage’s Analytical Engine.

hook: The first hard drive weighed over a ton
fact: The first hard drive, the IBM 350 (1956), stored 3.75 MB and weighed more than a ton.
detail: A 1 TB microSD card, under one gram, stores over 250,000 times more.

fact: 0.999… with 9s going on forever is exactly equal to 1. It’s not an approximation.
In a group of just 23 people, there’s a better than even chance that two share a birthday.
detail: It’s the birthday paradox: with 70 people, it’s over 99%.

hook: This shuffle is one of a kind
fact: A deck of 52 cards can be ordered in 52! ≈ 8 × 10⁶⁷ ways. A good shuffle has probably never happened before.
detail: That’s more than the number of atoms on Earth.

fact: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach the Earth.
detail: When you look at the Sun, you see it as it was 8 minutes ago.

hook: On Venus, a day > a year
fact: A day on Venus (243 Earth days) lasts longer than its year (225 Earth days).
detail: Venus also spins in the opposite direction to most planets.

fact: Astronauts on the International Space Station see about 16 sunrises every day.
detail: The ISS circles the Earth in about 90 minutes.

fact: The human heart beats about 100,000 times a day, more than 2.5 billion times in a lifetime.
detail: It pumps about 7,000 litres of blood every day.

hook: 2 metres of DNA in every cell
fact: The DNA in a single human cell, stretched out, is about 2 metres long.
detail: Yet it fits in a nucleus a few thousandths of a millimetre wide.

fact: Your body has roughly as many bacteria (≈ 38 trillion) as human cells (≈ 30 trillion).
detail: Most of them live in your gut.

fact: Helium was discovered in the Sun in 1868, from its light during an eclipse, before it was found on Earth in 1895.
detail: Its name comes from the Greek “helios”, the Sun.

fact: Diamond and the graphite in a pencil are made of the same element: carbon.
detail: Only the way the atoms are arranged changes everything.

fact: Water is one of the few substances that is lighter as a solid than as a liquid. That’s why ice floats.
detail: Otherwise, lakes would freeze from the bottom up.

fact: Divide 72 by the interest rate to get the number of years it takes to double your money. At 6%, about 12 years.
detail: It’s a shortcut widely used in finance.

fact: 1,000 dirhams invested at 7% a year become about 7,600 dirhams in 30 years, without adding anything.
detail: The interest earns interest of its own.

fact: The first modern stock exchange was born in Amsterdam in 1602, trading shares of the Dutch East India Company.
detail: It was also the first company to sell shares to the public.

fact: In the 14th century, Ibn Khaldun already described the division of labour and explained that taxes set too high reduce state revenue.
detail: Economist Arthur Laffer cited him as a source for his famous curve.

fact: The word “economy” comes from the Greek “oikonomia”: managing a household.
detail: “Oikos” = house, “nomos” = rule.

fact: Adam Smith published “The Wealth of Nations” in 1776, often seen as the first modern economics book.
detail: In it he describes the market’s “invisible hand”.

fact: Arabic is written from right to left, but numbers are read from left to right.
detail: In “٢٠٢٦” you read the thousands digit first.

fact: The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters, and each one can change shape depending on its place in the word.
detail: Alone, at the start, middle or end: up to 4 shapes.

fact: The word “zero” comes from the Arabic “ṣifr” (empty), through Italian.
detail: “Cipher” comes from the same Arabic word.

fact: The French word “oiseau” (bird) has all 5 vowels a, e, i, o, u in just 6 letters.
detail: Few French words manage it with so few letters.

hook: A word that reads both ways
fact: “Ressasser” (to keep going over) is a palindrome: it reads the same from left to right and right to left.
detail: Other examples: “kayak”, “radar”, “été”.

fact: “Anticonstitutionnellement” (25 letters) is one of the longest words in French.
detail: It means: in a way that goes against the Constitution.

fact: “Strengths” is one of the longest English words with only one vowel: 9 letters, just one “e”.
detail: Try saying it fast three times!

fact: “The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog” uses every letter of the English alphabet.
detail: A sentence like this is called a pangram.

fact: “E” is the most common letter in English.
detail: The most common word is “the”.

fact: Spanish is the 2nd most spoken native language in the world, with nearly 500 million native speakers.
detail: Only Mandarin Chinese has more.

fact: In Spanish, an upside-down question or exclamation mark opens the sentence: ¿Cómo estás?
detail: The Real Academia Española has recommended them since 1754.

fact: About 4,000 Spanish words come from Arabic: azúcar (sugar), aceite (oil), almohada (pillow)…
detail: “Ojalá” (hopefully) comes from “wa šāʾ Allāh”.

fact: The first message sent on ARPANET in 1969 was meant to be “LOGIN”. The system crashed after “LO”.
detail: ARPANET is the ancestor of the internet.

hook: The very first website still exists
fact: The first website, created by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1991, is still online: info.cern.ch
detail: It explained… how the Web works.

fact: The Python language isn’t named after the snake, but after the British comedy group Monty Python.
detail: Its creator, Guido van Rossum, was a fan of their show.

fact: The word “algorithm” comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, a 9th-century mathematician in Baghdad.
detail: The word “algebra” comes from his book, al-jabr.

fact: Our digits came from India, passed through the Arab world, and Fibonacci introduced them to Europe in 1202.
detail: He learned them as a boy in Béjaïa (Bugia), Algeria.

fact: If you could fold a 0.1 mm sheet of paper 42 times, it would be thicker than the distance to the Moon.
detail: 0.1 mm × 2⁴² ≈ 440,000 km. The Moon is 384,400 km away.

fact: Atoms are almost entirely empty. Without that empty space, all of humanity would fit in a sugar cube.
detail: Almost all of an atom’s mass is in its tiny nucleus.

fact: A lightning bolt can reach about 30,000 °C, roughly 5 times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
detail: The Sun’s surface is about 5,500 °C.

hook: In space, no one can hear you
fact: Sound needs matter to travel. In the vacuum of space, an explosion is completely silent.
detail: Light, on the other hand, travels perfectly through a vacuum.

fact: The octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
detail: Its blood uses copper (hemocyanin) instead of iron.

fact: The smallest bone in the human body is the stapes, in the ear. It’s about 3 mm long.
detail: It passes sound vibrations to the inner ear.

fact: About half of the Earth’s oxygen is produced by phytoplankton in the oceans.
detail: They are microscopic organisms that photosynthesise.

hook: A metal that melts in your hand
fact: Gallium is a metal that melts at 29.8 °C: it melts in your hand.
detail: It’s used in LEDs and solar panels.

fact: The periodic table now has 118 confirmed elements.
detail: The last ones added (2016): nihonium, moscovium, tennessine and oganesson.

fact: About 96% of the human body’s mass is made of 4 elements: oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen.
detail: Oxygen alone makes up about 65%.

fact: The word “bank” comes from the Italian “banca”, the bench of money changers.
detail: “Bankrupt” comes from “banca rotta”: a broken bench.

fact: The first banknotes appeared in China in the 11th century, under the Song dynasty.
detail: Europe only adopted them centuries later.

fact: On May 22, 2010, a programmer paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas: the first known purchase with bitcoin.
detail: The day is celebrated every year as Bitcoin Pizza Day.

fact: In 2008, Zimbabwe printed a 100-trillion-dollar banknote because of hyperinflation.
detail: It wasn’t enough to buy a bus ticket.
source: Banque centrale du Zimbabwe / Steve Hanke

fact: In 1946 Hungary, prices doubled roughly every 15 hours: the worst hyperinflation in history.
detail: The pengő was replaced by the forint.

fact: Water is vital but cheap; diamonds are useless for survival but very expensive. This is the water–diamond paradox.
detail: Scarcity matters more than usefulness in setting prices.

fact: Many English words come from Arabic: sugar (sukkar), coffee (qahwa), magazine (makhāzin), algebra (al-jabr).
detail: There are hundreds of them in everyday English.

fact: The word “hazard” comes from the Arabic “az-zahr”, which meant a die used in games.
detail: “Alcohol” also comes from Arabic (al-kuḥl).

fact: The oldest university still operating in the world is Al Quaraouiyine in Fez, founded in 859 by Fatima al-Fihri.
detail: It is recognised by Guinness World Records and UNESCO.

fact: French is spoken by about 321 million people on 5 continents.
detail: It’s the 5th most spoken language in the world.

fact: The Académie française was founded in 1635 by Cardinal Richelieu. Its 40 members are called “the Immortals”.
detail: Its mission: to look after the French language.

fact: “The Little Prince” is the most translated book in the world after religious texts: over 500 languages and dialects.
detail: It was written by Antoine de Saint-Exupéry in 1943.

fact: In the Oxford English Dictionary, the verb “run” has more than 600 different meanings.
detail: Run a race, run a company, run out of time…

fact: English is the international language of aviation: pilots and air traffic controllers on international flights must speak it.
detail: This is required by ICAO, the UN aviation agency.

fact: Shakespeare is credited with the first recorded use of hundreds of words, like “bedroom”, “lonely” and “eyeball”.
detail: Many of his expressions are still used every day.

hook: Ñ, a letter of its own
fact: “Ñ” is a full letter of the Spanish alphabet, as in “España” or “año”.
detail: It comes from a small “n” written above another “n”.

fact: The country with the most Spanish speakers isn’t Spain but Mexico, with about 130 million.
detail: Spain has about 48 million.

fact: “Don Quixote” by Cervantes, published in 1605, is often considered the first modern novel.
detail: It’s one of the best-selling books in history.

fact: The first .com domain, symbolics.com, was registered on March 15, 1985.
detail: Today there are more than 150 million .com domains.

hook: The QR code came from… cars
fact: The QR code was invented in 1994 in Japan by Denso Wave to track car parts.
detail: QR stands for “Quick Response”.

fact: The word “robot” comes from the Czech “robota”, forced labour. It first appeared in 1920 in Karel Čapek’s play R.U.R.
detail: It was his brother Josef Čapek who suggested the word.

fact: There are infinitely many prime numbers. Euclid proved it more than 2,300 years ago.
detail: His proof is still taught today.

fact: We know over 100 trillion digits of π, but 37 are enough to measure the universe to within an atom.
detail: NASA uses only 15 for its interplanetary calculations.

fact: The “=” sign was invented in 1557 by Robert Recorde, because “no two things can be more equal” than two parallel lines.
detail: Before that, people wrote “is equal to” in full.
source: The Whetstone of Witte, R. Recorde (1557)

hook: A teaspoon of star = 1 billion tons
fact: A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh about a billion tons.
detail: A neutron star is the size of a city but heavier than the Sun.

fact: Without corrections from Einstein’s relativity, GPS would drift by about 10 km every day.
detail: Satellite clocks run 38 microseconds a day faster.

hook: The speed of light is exact
fact: The speed of light is exactly 299,792,458 m/s. It isn’t measured: it defines the metre.
detail: Since 1983, the metre has been defined from the speed of light.

fact: The brain is about 2% of your body weight but uses about 20% of its energy.
detail: It keeps using energy even while you sleep.

hook: A baby has more bones than you
fact: A baby is born with about 300 bones. Adults have only 206, because some fuse as we grow.
detail: The skull, for example, starts in several pieces.

hook: Dolphins sleep with half a brain
fact: Dolphins sleep with only one half of their brain at a time. The other half stays awake.
detail: That way they can keep breathing and watch for danger.

fact: Firework colours come from metals: strontium for red, barium for green, copper for blue, sodium for yellow.
detail: Each element gives off light of a precise colour.

hook: Salt: an explosive metal + a toxic gas
fact: Table salt is made of sodium, a metal that explodes in water, and chlorine, a toxic gas.
detail: Together they form sodium chloride, NaCl.

fact: Your stomach contains hydrochloric acid, with a pH between 1 and 2.
detail: The stomach wall protects itself with a layer of mucus.

fact: There will never be more than 21 million bitcoins: the limit is written into its code.
detail: The last bitcoin should be created around 2140.

fact: Warren Buffett bought his first stock at age 11.
detail: He became one of the richest investors in the world.

fact: With 2% inflation a year, prices double in about 35 years.
detail: That’s why saving without investing loses purchasing power.

fact: Economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed that about 80% of the land in Italy was owned by 20% of the people.
detail: This 80/20 rule is now used everywhere.

fact: Monopoly comes from “The Landlord’s Game”, invented by Lizzie Magie in 1904 to show the dangers of monopolies.
detail: The game was later reworked and sold as Monopoly.

hook: The Big Mac, an economist’s tool
fact: Since 1986, The Economist has compared the price of a Big Mac around the world to measure currency values.
detail: It’s the “Big Mac Index” of purchasing power parity.

fact: Arabic is one of the 6 official languages of the UN. World Arabic Language Day is December 18.
detail: It is spoken by more than 400 million people.

fact: In Arabic, short vowels usually aren’t written. They’re added as marks (ḥarakāt) in the Quran and children’s books.
detail: Experienced readers work them out from context.

fact: The word “admiral” comes from the Arabic “amīr”, meaning leader or commander.
detail: You find it again in “emir”.
